title: BERT and pretraining
text:
CHAPTER 18. TRANSFORMERS
SECTION 18.2. BERT AND PRETRAINING

Within about eighteen months of the transformer paper, natural language processing changed its basic method. Instead of training a new model for each task from scratch on a small labeled dataset, researchers pretrained one large model on huge amounts of unlabeled text and then fine-tuned it for each task with little data. ImageNet pretraining had done something similar for vision (Section 16.2). The model that made this approach dominant was Google's BERT, released in October 2018. This section explains the pretraining idea, BERT's objectives and architecture, its results, and the family of models that followed.

1. From word vectors to pretrained networks

Word embeddings (Section 17.1) were already a kind of pretraining: learn vectors from unlabeled text, then use them as the first layer of a task model. But they gave each word a single vector regardless of context, and the rest of the network still had to be trained for each task. Around 2015-2018, several groups pretrained whole networks:

  - Andrew Dai and Quoc Le (2015) pretrained LSTMs as language models or sequence autoencoders and fine-tuned them for text classification.
  - ELMo (Matthew Peters and colleagues, Allen Institute for AI; arXiv February 2018) trained a two-layer bidirectional LSTM language model on about a billion words and used a learned combination of its internal states as contextual word representations, added to existing task models. "Bank" now got different vectors in "river bank" and "bank loan." ELMo improved the state of the art on six varied tasks.
  - ULMFiT (Jeremy Howard and Sebastian Ruder, January 2018) showed that fine-tuning a whole pretrained LSTM language model, with techniques such as discriminative learning rates and gradual unfreezing, worked very well for text classification with few labels.
  - OpenAI's GPT (Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans and Ilya Sutskever, "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training," June 2018) pretrained a 12-layer transformer decoder as a left-to-right language model on books (the BooksCorpus) and fine-tuned it on downstream tasks, improving the state of the art on 9 of the 12 tasks it studied (Section 18.3).

The common recipe: pretrain with a self-supervised objective, where labels come from the text itself, then fine-tune.

2. BERT

Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee and Kristina Toutanova of Google AI Language posted "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding" on arXiv on 11 October 2018 (published at NAACL 2019), and Google released code and pretrained models at the end of October 2018. BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.

The key point is bidirectionality. A left-to-right language model like GPT predicts each word only from the words before it, so its representation of a word cannot use what comes after. ELMo combined separately trained left-to-right and right-to-left models, but the two directions did not interact inside the network. BERT used a transformer encoder (Section 18.1), in which every position attends to all positions on both sides, in every layer. The problem is that a standard language modeling objective is impossible with full bidirectional attention: each word could simply "see itself." BERT solved this with a different objective.

3. Pretraining objectives

Masked language modeling (MLM). Choose 15 percent of the token positions in each sequence at random. Of these, replace 80 percent with a special [MASK] token, 10 percent with a random token, and leave 10 percent unchanged. The model must predict the original token at each chosen position, with a cross-entropy loss on those positions only. (The 80-10-10 split reduces the mismatch between pretraining, where [MASK] appears, and fine-tuning, where it never does.) Example: "the cat sat on the [MASK]" with target "mat." This is a version of the "cloze" test from psychology and education (Wilson Taylor, 1953).

Next sentence prediction (NSP). Given two segments A and B, predict whether B actually followed A in the original text (50 percent of the time) or is a random segment from the corpus (50 percent). The goal was to learn relations between sentences, useful for question answering and inference. Later work (RoBERTa, below) found NSP unnecessary or slightly harmful.

Input format. Each input begins with a special [CLS] token, segments are separated by [SEP], and each token's input is the sum of a WordPiece token embedding (a vocabulary of about 30,000 subwords), a learned position embedding (up to 512 positions) and a segment embedding (A or B). The final hidden state of [CLS] serves as a summary for classification.

4. Model sizes and training

Two sizes:

    BERT-Base:  L = 12 layers, H = 768 hidden size, A = 12 heads, 110M parameters
    BERT-Large: L = 24 layers, H = 1024 hidden size, A = 16 heads, 340M parameters

(BERT-Base matched GPT's size so the two could be compared.) A quick check for BERT-Base: each layer has about 4 H^2 attention weights and 2 x H x 4H feedforward weights, 12 H^2 in total, about 7.1 million; 12 layers give about 85 million; the token embeddings add about 30,522 x 768, about 23 million, for roughly 109 million, matching 110M.

Pretraining data: BooksCorpus (800 million words) plus English Wikipedia (2,500 million words; text passages only, without lists and tables). BERT-Large was trained on 16 Cloud TPUs (64 TPU chips) in Google's Pod configuration, and each pretraining run took 4 days, according to the paper. This was a large cost for academic labs at the time, but after Google released the trained weights, anyone could fine-tune them cheaply: the paper notes that all its results could be reproduced in at most 1 hour on a single Cloud TPU, or a few hours on a GPU, starting from the pretrained model.

5. Fine-tuning

To adapt BERT to a task, add a small output layer and train all parameters on the task's labeled data for a few epochs:

  - Sentence or sentence-pair classification (sentiment, entailment): a softmax layer on the [CLS] vector.
  - Token tagging (named entities): a classifier on each token's output vector.
  - Extractive question answering (SQuAD): input the question and a passage; learn start and end vectors S and E, and predict the answer span from softmax(S . T_i) for the start and softmax(E . T_j) for the end, where T_i is the output vector of token i.

The architecture is the same for all tasks; only the small head changes. This "one model, many tasks" approach replaced a decade of task-specific architectures.

6. Results

BERT obtained new state-of-the-art results on eleven NLP tasks. From the abstract: the GLUE benchmark score rose to 80.5 (a 7.7 point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7 percent, SQuAD v1.1 test F1 to 93.2 and SQuAD v2.0 test F1 to 83.1. GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation, Alex Wang and colleagues, 2018) combined nine tasks, including sentiment, paraphrase and entailment; SQuAD (Stanford Question Answering Dataset, Pranav Rajpurkar and colleagues, 2016) asked for answer spans in Wikipedia paragraphs. Ablations showed that bidirectionality and model size both mattered: larger models were better even on small datasets, a sign of what scaling would bring.

The result spread fast. In October 2019, Google announced it was using BERT in Search, saying it would help Search better understand one in ten searches in the U.S. in English. By 2020, BERT-style models were standard in industry for classification, search ranking and information extraction, and the open-source Hugging Face Transformers library made pretrained models easy to download and fine-tune.

7. Successors and refinements

  - RoBERTa (Yinhan Liu and colleagues, Facebook AI, July 2019) showed BERT was undertrained: training longer on more data (about 160 GB of text), with bigger batches, dynamic masking, and without NSP, gave clearly better results with the same architecture.
  - ALBERT (2019) shared parameters across layers and factorized the embedding matrix to shrink the model.
  - DistilBERT (Hugging Face, 2019) used knowledge distillation (training a small "student" model to match a large "teacher's" output distributions, Hinton and colleagues, 2015) to keep most of BERT's accuracy with a smaller, faster model.
  - ELECTRA (Kevin Clark and colleagues, 2020) replaced MLM with "replaced token detection": a small generator fills in masked tokens, and the main model learns to detect which tokens were replaced, learning from every position rather than only the 15 percent masked.
  - Encoder-decoder pretraining: T5 (Colin Raffel and colleagues, Google, October 2019) cast every task as text-to-text ("translate English to German: ...", "summarize: ...") and pretrained on C4, a cleaned Common Crawl corpus of about 750 GB, with a span-corruption objective; BART (Facebook, 2019) pretrained a denoising encoder-decoder.
  - Multilingual models (multilingual BERT, XLM-R) trained on text in about 100 languages, and showed surprising cross-lingual transfer: fine-tune in English, test in another language.

8. Encoders versus decoders

BERT-style encoders excel at understanding tasks with fixed outputs, and they are still widely used, for example as embedding models for search and retrieval. But they cannot naturally generate text. After 2020, the largest efforts shifted to decoder-only models like GPT, for reasons explained in Section 18.3: a single generative model can perform tasks from instructions or examples given in its input, without any fine-tuning, and its abilities grow steadily with scale. In effect, the "pretrain then fine-tune" paradigm of BERT evolved into "pretrain, then prompt or instruction-tune" (Chapter 19).

9. What pretraining learns

Probing studies ("BERTology") found that BERT's layers encode a surprising amount of linguistic structure: part-of-speech information in lower layers, syntactic relationships in middle layers (some attention heads track specific dependency relations, such as verbs attending to their objects), and more semantic information in higher layers. Ian Tenney and colleagues (2019) described this as BERT "rediscovering the classical NLP pipeline." BERT also absorbed factual associations and social biases from its training text, and its success on benchmarks sometimes relied on shallow cues in the datasets, a warning that benchmark scores can overstate understanding.

10. Summary

  - Pretraining on unlabeled text and fine-tuning on small labeled sets became NLP's standard method in 2018 (ELMo, ULMFiT, GPT, BERT).
  - BERT (Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova, Google, October 2018) is a bidirectional transformer encoder pretrained with masked language modeling (15 percent of tokens, 80-10-10) and next sentence prediction.
  - BERT-Base: 12 layers, 768 hidden, 110M parameters; BERT-Large: 24 layers, 1024 hidden, 340M; trained on BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia (3.3 billion words).
  - It set new results on eleven tasks (GLUE 80.5, SQuAD v1.1 F1 93.2) and entered Google Search in 2019.
  - RoBERTa, ALBERT, DistilBERT, ELECTRA, T5 and BART refined pretraining; generative decoder-only models then took the lead for general-purpose AI.
